The Arawan family comprises six languages from southern Amazonia, namely, Paumari, Deni, Kulina, Sorowaha, Arawa and Madi (Dixon 1995: 263). Madi can be further divided into three mutually intelligible, closely related dialects (with over 95% shared vocabulary). These are known as Jarawara, Jamamadi and Banawa (Dixon 1995: 291). See Vogel (1989) for an earlier analysis of gender marking in Jarawara.
As in Dixon (2000; 2004), the inherent gender of a noun is signalled in parentheses in the gloss, and contextual gender values on agreement targets are glossed like other inflectional features.
The ungrammatical agreement alternatives must be inferred from Dixon’s (2000; 2004) discussion of the data since negative evidence seldom features in the source material.

The use of default verbal agreement forms with first and second person pronouns is also attested elsewhere in the Arawan languages (Bond 2019), and Baerman (2023: 11–13) catalogues similar patterns cross-linguistically, including in Nakh-Daghestanian (Chumakina et al. 2007), Tucanoan (Baerman & Corbett 2013; Chacon & Michael 2018), Omotic (Baerman 2020) and Kadu (Baerman 2023) languages.

When citing the gender agreement forms of third person singular PNs (e.g. mano/mani ‘arm’), I always list the masculine agreement form first, since stems homophonous with this form are more pervasive within the paradigm than those homophonous with the feminine agreement stem. This contrasts with the order in Dixon (2004) where feminine agreement forms are cited first in lists (e.g. mani/mano ‘arm’).

Nearly all nouns proper in Jarawara have an inherent grammatical gender: masculine or feminine. According to Dixon (2000: 496), there are a handful of nouns which can control agreement in either gender, depending on the sex of the referent, including habai ‘friend’, inamatewe ‘child’, and jibotee ‘spouse’. In contrast, I propose that PNs lack an inherent gender value (§2.2), but see Dixon (2004) and Adamson (2024) for a different view.

Note that PNs, like inanimates in general, do not express inherent number, nor do they directly control contextual expressions of number on the predicate (Dixon 2004: 290). See §4.1 for further discussion.

Adpositions are a common source of possession marking (see Heine 1997: 144–158 for examples). For more on the possible diachrony of Jarawara alienable possession constructions see Stassen (2009: 126–7).

While PNs are typically accompanied by a possessor, text data in Dixon (2004) demonstrates that third person singular PNs can be used without overt possessors (see §4.2.3). This is distinct from the usage of non-relational ‘free nouns’ that are etymologically related to a subset of PNs (see Dixon 2004: 312).
Kinship terms, while inherently relational, do not fall within the class of PNs. See Dixon (2004: 298–301) for discussion of their properties.

Possessed nouns behave like other inanimate nouns in that they cannot be specified for number with the nominal modifier mee (cf. the third person pronoun mee), nor are PNs followed by mee in the predicate (Dixon 2004: 290).

While I assume that PNs in Jarawara do not have an inherent gender value, it is possible that this was not always so since inalienably possessed nouns in the Arawan language Paumari (Chapman & Derbyshire 1986) agree with their possessor and simultaneously have their own inherent gender value.
This is a somewhat unusual claim from a typological perspective, since first and second person pronouns rarely have an inherent gender. See Baerman (2020) for discussion and references to examples.

Dixon (2004: 65–66) suggests that inclusion of epenthetic /w/ in the second singular form, where we might otherwise expect tifi based on other vowel hiatus rules makes these forms distinct from those predicted by other attested phonological processes. If we follow his view, it indicates that selection of the wifi stem is morphologically, not phonologically conditioned.
See Adamson (2024), discussed in §5, for an approach that relies on postsyntactic impoverishment rules that delete features values to enable an analysis involving natural classes.

While there is a thematic restriction on what sorts of possessors can be ncomps, there does not seem to be a need to formalise this for Jarawara. I put aside this issue here and assume the ncomps can thematically restricted in the same way that objects can, if required.

Sometimes this stem differs from that used for third person singular masculine. For instance, in oko sowi ‘my penis’ (cf. Dixon 2000: 351) the stem sowi differs from the stem sowiri used elsewhere in the paradigm. See §3.1.7, Table 8.

The PNs narabo/narabi and warabo/warabi ‘his/her ear’ are in apparent free variation in Jarawara. The forms narabo/narabi are found in the neighbouring Jamamadí variety, while warabo/warabi occur in the Banawá variety (Dixon 2004: 348).

Feature sharing accounts might also prove appropriate for agreement in Tundra Nenets possessive constructions, and possibly some other languages of northern Eurasia (see Nikolaeva 2014b, Nichols 2017).

Although I have not done so here, it would be entirely possible to write a single entry for mano with disjunctive sets of ncomp feature values that accounts for both (28) and (33) if this were considered the most appropriate way to capture the morphomic distribution of the stem.
See Dienst (2014: 81–82) for discussion of similar recursive structures in the related language Kulina.
